edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' (page id in place of the bare right-hand page number) on all six K-1 pages; this is one template change.

edits.quote: Draw each way on a small shape. [eight recording hexagons at half scale, triangle edge about 0.5 inch, 16 triangles each]
edits.fix: Kindergartners cannot draw 8 rhombi cleanly on half-inch triangles. Enlarge the recording shapes to about 0.75-inch edges (six or seven fit if the free lower third of the page is used), or say 'color each block a different color' so the record is made by coloring pairs of triangles. The big board is correct at actual size and has 6 coverings.

k-1.summary: Six concrete, correct problems on actual-size boards: covered and uncoverable shapes, including an even-area shape that cannot be covered (the 8-triangle trapezoid with 5 up and 3 down triangles); fewest greens in triangles of side 2, 3 and 4 (2, 3, 4); find all coverings (2 and 3 ways, then 6); fewest blocks (3, 3, 4); and a last-block game whose answers are first, second, first, first, second. It is a full hour of real work for K-1, not a watered-down sheet. The organizer only needs to fix the footer and enlarge the Problem 6 recording shapes.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on all seven pages.

edits.quote: [page 4: the side-5 triangle with its box and five writing lines, with no problem label]
edits.fix: The side-5 board has to go on its own page at actual size, but a child who turns to page 4 sees an unlabeled triangle. Label it as the continuation of Problem 3 (for example 'Problem 3, continued') so it is clear the box and the explanation belong to Problem 3.

edits.quote: Imagine a triangle board with 10 small triangles along each side. If you cover it with blue rhombuses and green triangles, what is the fewest number of green triangles you need? What if the board has 100 small triangles along each side?
edits.fix: Once the Problem 3 boxes read 2, 3, 4, 5, a child answers 10 and 100 from the pattern in under a minute, so this numbered problem does not support five minutes of work. Either make it the last question of Problem 3, or ask the child to show why the side-10 board needs exactly 10 (55 up against 45 down, plus a covering that leaves only 10).

grades-2-3.summary: A strong development of kernel 1 in which every diagram and answer checks out. P1 has odd-area and up/down-imbalance boards (the star and the 2-1-1 hexagon can be covered; the side-3 triangle and the 12-triangle trapezoid cannot). P2 has holes: E has two up holes, F is an hourglass whose counts balance but which still cannot be covered, and G can be covered 4 ways. P3 has the n-greens triangles with a proof. P5 compares chevrons with blues: 4, 5, 4, 5 against 2, 3, 4, 5. P6 is an extremal design problem (6 is exactly the most a connected 20-triangle board can need), and P7 is the up/down rule, which holds for all 144 up-down placements. The only edits are the footer, the unlabeled continuation page and the thin Problem 4.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on all seven pages.

edits.quote: On the small boards below, draw all your coverings from Problem 1 again. Draw a line between two coverings whenever one flip changes one into the other.
edits.fix: Copying the 6 coverings a second time is busywork. Also, in the 2-by-4 grid the connecting lines will cross other boards. Have children label their Problem 1 drawings with letters and draw the flip graph on letters spread out on this page, or lay out the Problem 1 recording boards so they have room for connecting lines, and then delete the eight duplicate boards. (The answer is a graph on 6 coverings with 6 flips; the two extreme coverings are 4 flips apart.)

edits.quote: Start with any covering of the hexagon board from Problem 3. Make flips, one at a time, until you are back at the covering you started with. Find a way to do this with 4 flips that never flips the same hexagon twice in a row.
edits.fix: From the two extreme coverings (E and F of Problem 3) no 4-flip round trip avoids flipping the same hexagon twice in a row: only one flip is possible there, so the walk has to come straight back. F is exactly what is left on the board after Problem 3. 18 of the 20 coverings work. Write 'Choose a covering...' and name a starting covering that works (for example A), or add the question of which coverings it is possible from.

edits.quote: [two writing lines are the only recording space for a 4-flip round trip]
edits.fix: Add four or five small copies of the hexagon board in a row, so children can draw the covering after each flip, or ask them to shade the hexagon they flip at each step.

edits.quote: Write the ribbon of each covering of the board from Problem 1. On the hexagon board each covering has two ribbons, because its top side has two short edges. Find exactly what one flip does to the ribbons.
edits.fix: The Problem 1 board is also a hexagon, so 'the hexagon board' is ambiguous. Write 'On the board from Problem 3, each covering has two ribbons...' and say which board(s) to use to find what a flip does to the ribbons.

edits.quote: Draw them on the small hexagons below [25 hexagons with triangle edges of about 0.3 inch]
edits.fix: Drawing 20 coverings of 12 rhombi each on 0.3-inch triangles is cramped and slow. Enlarge the hexagons to about 0.4–0.45-inch edges in a 4-by-5 or 4-by-6 grid, or allow children to record each covering by its two ribbons.

grades-4-5.summary: An excellent kernel-2 sequence, and the mathematics checks out throughout. P1 has 6 coverings, and in P2 the two extreme coverings are 4 flips apart. The P3 coverings are drawn correctly, with fewest flips A to B 3, C to D 4 and E to F 8. Round trips can take 4 flips but never 5 or 7. The ribbon example LRRLR is drawn correctly. Both ribbons of E are RRLL and both ribbons of F are LLRR, which gives the lower bound of 8. P7 and P8 each count 20 coverings. The edits are about page execution: the duplicate drawing in P2, the 'any covering' prompt in P4 that fails from E and F, missing recording space in P4, ambiguous board names in P5, and the tiny P7 grids.

overall.strongest: The grades 2–3 pages carry kernel 1 from possible/impossible boards through holes, fewest-green triangles, chevrons, an extremal design problem and the up/down rule, with every diagram correct and almost nothing to cut.
overall.weakest: The grades 4–5 pages need the most work. The mathematics there is excellent, but there is a redraw step in Problem 2, a Problem 4 prompt that cannot be done from the coverings children will most likely start with (E or F), and cramped or missing recording space.
